explanation: No consistent trigger: the strong activations are spread over unrelated tokens in German, Russian, Chinese and English prose, code identifiers, a URL '?', and digits. Seeing the token or its context gives no reliable way to predict the activation.

Fires on function words, mostly 'the', 'a', 'an' and 'of', and sometimes on a word-piece or digit that comes right after a verb or preposition and opens a noun phrase (e.g. 'members of [the]', 'about [an] hour', 'close to [1],500'). Strongest when the article sits mid-sentence after a preposition or verb. Weak on sentence-initial 'The'.

Strongest on 'subject' in the license boilerplate 'This source file is subject to ...' (Zend/Magento PHP headers). It also fires moderately to strongly on mixed tokens in technical or math text: operators in algebra problems, indentation whitespace in code, and technical nouns ('method', 'neighborhood', 'missiles').

Fires on the slot after an encyclopedic classification phrase, mostly in Wikipedia-style stub articles: 'described' in 'Category:Moths described in' / 'It was described by', 'in' in 'is a moth in the family', and the space before a year in 'is a 1960 film/album'. It also fires moderately on verbs taking a criterion ('meet the criteria', 'referring to').

Fires on tokens inside programming or technical Q&A text: assertion method calls ('t.equal', '.assertEqual', '.should'), error-message words ('No suitable driver', 'no known class'), path pieces, code comments, and technical terms in a question title. It also fires on technical nouns in scientific abstracts ('visual analogue', 'resolution'). Plain prose stays low.

Fires mostly on subword fragments inside rare or foreign words and names ('D'ALESSAND', 'antiproliferative', 'Jabodetabek', 'Dalmatia', 'tetrahedron') and on tokens in non-English text (Portuguese, French, Spanish, Hindi). It also fires on a few code tokens. Common English words stay weak.

One isolated peak on a digit inside a negative-number answer in an arithmetic dataset ('-[1]0379'). Otherwise moderate activation on mixed tokens: 'its' in 'Inc. and its affiliates', name pieces of Korean or ancient names, header-guard identifiers, and commas. No common thread.

Fires on words that refer the reader to another source or link: 'more' in 'Learn more' / 'See more' / 'Read More', 'see', 'here' in 'see here', and 'http(s)' after 'See' or inside a markdown link. It also fires on license-header metadata such as '-Identifier' in 'SPDX-License-Identifier' and '(' in 'Copyright (c)'.

Fires on structural tokens in Go source and other generated code: 'package' after the license header, '.com' in 'github.com' import paths, 'go-swagger', func/import syntax ('func (', 'import ('), and similar boilerplate in Python setup and docstring files. It also fires on line breaks in short poems and on a few scattered word-pieces.

No clear common feature. The strong activations mix the endings of uncommon words ('complacency', 'rarefied', 'poppycock”'), variables in algebra problems, 'Before' in a legal header, 'Developer tools', and prepositions such as 'of' and 'while'.

Fires on the head noun of a field, sport or industry, mostly football or soccer ('American soccer player', 'footballer', 'ice hockey', 'Fútbol') and 'estate' in 'real estate'. It also fires on 'beekeeping', and weakly to moderately on other professional fields ('investment banker', 'acting', 'botanist', 'architecture').

Fires on early word-pieces of a word that has been split into subword tokens. The clearest cases are 'unt' in 'untimely', 'untangles' and 'untold', plus pieces of rare names and technical terms ('Nauvoo', 'lymphokines', 'Ayodhya', 'euphoric') and of Portuguese words. Activation is driven by the fragment, not the context.

Mostly fires on function words inside fixed multiword phrases: 'of' in 'one of', 'some of', 'out of'; 'any' in 'in any case'; 'much' in 'much better'; 'not' in 'were it not'; 'or may not'. It also fires on code tokens such as indentation and 'new'/'Thread' after '='. The phrase context matters more than the token itself.

Fires in source code at the slot just before a value or definition: assignment and mapping punctuation ('=>', '=', ':' after an object key such as 'success:'), string quotes that open an argument, 'public' at the start of a method declaration, and indentation before a declaration. Mostly JavaScript/PHP/Java/C#, plus stack traces ('in `require''). It does not fire on prose.
